transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I suppose I should start from the beginning, because it’s not just one thing, it’s a whole string of things that’s been going on. I came in today because... well, it started down at the domino table. I go down there most days, have been for years since I stopped working, just sitting with the other fellas. But lately, the men at the table, they’ve been slipping these little messages into the conversation. Just... little things that are meant for me. 

And it’s not just them, either, which is what really got me thinking. I come home, I sit in my armchair, and I turn on the radio, and the announcer—the fella who does the afternoon segment—he does the exact same thing. He puts these little messages right there in the broadcast, directed right at me. 

Now, I try to talk to my wife about it, and she just waves her hand at me. She says it’s just talk, says I’m getting worked up over nothing and that it's just regular conversation, but she’s not paying attention to the words they use. She doesn't hear the way they pause. I know what’s going on. Even if she thinks it’s just chatter, I know they are warning me to be careful. I can feel it, doctor, the way they look at me over the dominoes, the tone of the radio man's voice... they're telling me to watch my step, and I just... I needed to tell somebody who might actually listen instead of just brushing it off like my wife does, because a man can't just ignore a warning like that, can he?
When you say they're sending you messages, do you feel like they're using words or phrases that only you would understand carry a special meaning?

Well, yes, exactly, doctor. It’s... it’s not like they come right out and say my name, no, no, it’s much more subtle than that. It’s the way they string the words together. Like... like the other day, Hector—he’s one of the fellas I play with, known him for fifteen years, maybe more, since before my knees gave out and I had to stop working—he slapped a double-six down on the table, looked right at me, and said, "Sometimes you gotta know when the house is built on sand." Now, to anyone else, to my wife, that’s just an old man talking nonsense over a game. But I know what he meant. He was telling me my foundation isn't safe. He was warning me. 

And then, not two hours later, I’m sitting in my chair, listening to the afternoon sports broadcast, and the announcer—the one with the deep voice, he’s been on the air for a long time—he’s talking about a baseball game, right? But he pauses. A real long pause. And then he says, "You have to watch the blind spots, folks." Folks! But he wasn't talking to folks, doctor, he was talking to me. It’s these little phrases, these... these hidden warnings. My wife, she just sighs and tells me to turn the radio down, says I’m making mountains out of molehills. She says, "Oh, they’re just talking about the game, they’re just talking about dominoes." But she’s not listening, not really. She doesn't hear the weight behind the words. I know what they’re doing. They are warning me to be careful, doctor. I just... I just have to figure out what exactly I'm supposed to be careful of, you know? Because you can't just ignore a warning when it comes at you from two different places like that. It’s not just talk. It’s never just talk.
Do you think these messages are part of a larger plan or scheme directed specifically at you, like a coordinated effort to warn or harm you?

That’s exactly what I’m getting at, doctor. You hit the nail right on the head. See, like I was telling you just a minute ago, the whole reason I came in here today is because the men at the domino table and sometimes the radio announcer keep giving me these little messages that are meant just for me. And even when my wife says it is just talk and tries to shoo me away, I know they are warning me to be careful. 

And to answer your question, yes, it has to be some kind of coordinated thing, doesn't it? Because how else would Hector down at the tables and the sports announcer on the AM dial be singing from the exact same hymnal? It’s not a coincidence. I’ve lived eighty-four years on this earth, and I didn't get to be this old by ignoring things that are right in front of my face. I might not have a fancy education, I left school back in the eighth grade to help my daddy out, but I have common sense. And common sense tells me that when two completely different people in two completely different places start dropping the exact same hints... well, they’re in on it together. 

They have to be part of some larger plan. I don't know if they are the ones who want to harm me, or if they just know that someone else is coming to do it, but the warning is real. It is a real effort to get my attention. Even if my wife just brushes it off as old men gossiping, I know in my gut it is a plan. They are trying to tell me to watch my back, and it just drives me crazy that I can't get her to see the big picture here, because if they are going through all this trouble to coordinate these messages, something big must be coming.
Doctor: Have you noticed any messages being sent to you through other means, like television, newspapers, or objects around you, that others might not notice?

Well, now, television and newspapers... you know, I don't really watch a whole lot of television these days. The pictures flash too fast, it just gives me a headache, and all those commercials, they just shout at you, all that noise. And the newspaper, well, they make the print so small nowadays. Ever since I lost my good reading glasses a few years back, I just don't bother much with the daily paper, except maybe to check the weather if it looks like rain. So, no, I haven't seen anything in the papers or on the TV screen. I haven't noticed any objects doing anything strange either. 

But like I was explaining just a minute ago, doctor—and this is the whole reason I came in to see you today, the whole crux of the matter—it's the men at the domino table. Them, and sometimes that radio announcer. They're the ones giving me those little messages meant just for me. I don't need a newspaper to tell me what's going on when it's happening right in front of my face. I try to explain this to my wife, I really do, I sit her down and I say, 'Listen to what they're actually saying,' and even when she just sighs and says it is just talk, I know better. I know they are warning me to be careful. 

A man doesn't need a hidden message in a newspaper when he's already getting them loud and clear over a game of bones and the AM dial. It’s just... it’s frustrating, you know? When you know exactly what’s happening, and the person you’ve shared a home with for fifty years just brushes it off as regular talk. But I know a warning when I hear one, doctor. I don't need the television to confirm it.
Do you feel that these messages are threatening or harmful, or do they seem to be trying to help or warn you in some way?

Well, now, that’s the tricky part, doctor. That’s the part that keeps me up at night, staring at the ceiling fan going round and round. Are they trying to help me, or are they the ones I need to be worried about? I... I lean towards thinking it's a warning. Like they know something bad is coming down the pike and they're trying to give me a heads-up, but they can't just come out and say it plain. Like I told you, doctor, and this is the whole reason I’m sitting in this chair today, I came because the men at the domino table and sometimes the radio announcer give little messages meant just for me. 

And it’s a heavy burden, carrying that around. Knowing something is wrong, something is brewing, and you’re the only one who sees the storm clouds. I try to talk to my wife about it, I really do. Just yesterday morning, over a bowl of oatmeal, I said to her, "Did you hear what Hector said about the foundation?" And she just shook her head, poured herself more coffee, and told me I was letting my imagination run wild again. But even when my wife says it is just talk, I know they are warning me to be careful. 

Why else would they go through all that trouble? Hector, he’s a good man, known him for years. I don't think he wants to hurt me. I think he’s trying to do me a solid. And the announcer on the radio, well, he doesn't know me from Adam, but maybe he sees something I don't. Maybe he’s got a wider view of things. So, I think it's a warning, doctor. A warning to be careful. I just... I just wish I knew what exactly the danger was, because walking around waiting for the other shoe to drop, well, it’s no way for a man my age to live, I'll tell you that much.
Have you ever experienced any other unusual things that others around you don't seem to notice, like hearing voices when no one is speaking or seeing things that aren't really there?

Well, now, see, that's another thing that's been bothering me. And I don't know if it's connected to Hector and the radio man, or if it's just my old ears playing tricks on me, but... well, yes, I suppose I have. 

It happens mostly in the afternoons. You know how it gets around two or three o'clock? The sun is coming in through the front window, hitting the rug just right, and the whole house gets so quiet you can hear the dust settle. My wife usually takes a little nap around then, so I'm just sitting there in my chair, maybe resting my eyes for a minute. And then, clear as day, I hear him. 

I hear my old friend, Charlie. He passed on about five years ago, God rest his soul, but I hear him call my name right from the front porch. "Hey there, old timer," he'll say, just like he used to when he'd come over to borrow a tool or just chew the fat. And sometimes, it's not even talking. Sometimes I just hear him humming. He used to sing in the choir down at First Baptist, had a real nice baritone, and I'll hear him humming one of those old hymns. 

It sounds so real, doctor. It sounds like he is standing right there on the porch, waiting for me to open the screen door. The first few times it happened, I actually got up out of my chair—and my knees aren't what they used to be, let me tell you, it takes a minute to get moving—and I walked all the way to the front door, half expecting to see him standing there in his old overalls. But there's never anybody there. Just the empty porch and the street. 

I haven't told my wife about it. She already thinks I'm making too much out of the domino games, so if I tell her I'm hearing Charlie hum from the porch, she'll probably want to pack me off to a home. But I hear it, doctor. I know I do. And I don't see anything that isn't there, no ghosts or shadows or anything like that, but the hearing... yes. Just Charlie, calling my name or humming his choir songs, right there on the porch.
Have you ever had any other experiences where you believed something was happening or being directed at you that others didn’t seem to notice or agree with?

Well, let me sit and think on that a minute, doctor. Because a man my age, well, you see a lot of things over the years, and you want to be sure you're giving the whole picture. But as for right now, happening to me... no, I can't rightly say that there is anything else besides what we've already talked about. 

I mean, I told you all about Hector and the boys down at the domino table, and that fella on the AM radio. That's the main thing. That's what really fills up my mind most days and gets my heart beating faster than it ought to. But if I go down to the grocery store to pick up a carton of milk or a loaf of bread for the wife—she likes that soft white bread, you know, the kind in the plastic bag, says it's easier on her gums nowadays since she won't go back to the dentist to get her bridge fixed—well, the cashier there, she just rings me up regular. She doesn't give me any secret looks or try to pass me any messages with the receipt. It's just the price of the milk, and that's the end of it. 

And the mailman, he just drops off the light bill and the junk mail. He doesn't linger or try to signal me about anything brewing out there in the world. I sit on my porch—when I'm not hearing Charlie hum, like I was just explaining to you—and I watch the cars go by, and they're just cars. Just folks going to work or heading home to their own families. Nobody is flashing their headlights at me or honking in some kind of code. 

It's really just the dominoes and the radio, doctor. That's a heavy enough sack to carry, if you ask me. I don't need the whole neighborhood trying to get my attention, just the ones who know what's coming and are trying to give me that heads-up. So, no, beyond what we've already chewed over today, I haven't had any other things directed at me. Just the regular day-to-day quiet of an old man's life, except for those warnings I told you about.

Has this kind of thing—feeling like people are sending you secret messages or that you're hearing someone who isn't there—ever happened to you before, or is this something new that's only started recently?

Well, now, let me think back on that, doctor, because when you get to be eighty-four, time has a funny way of stretching out and bunching up, if you know what I mean. A year can feel like a month, and a month can feel like a whole lifetime. I had to sit and really chew on this exact thing the other day. I was looking at the calendar in the kitchen—the one with the pictures of covered bridges that the bank gives out every January—and I started counting back the pages. 

Because, you see, it wasn't happening last summer. I know that for a fact. Last summer, I was just sitting on the porch, complaining about the heat and swatting at mosquitoes, and Charlie wasn't humming, and Hector was just playing dominoes regular without any of that extra meaning behind it. But then... well, it was right around the time the weather started turning real cold last year. I remember because my wife made me get my heavy wool coat out of the cedar closet, the one that always smells like mothballs no matter how long you let it air out on the line. 

That's when I first started noticing the radio announcer slipping those warnings in between the weather and the news. And then, maybe a week or two after I got that coat out, I heard Charlie call my name from the porch for the very first time. So, if I'm doing the math right—and my head is still pretty sharp for numbers, even if I had to leave school before the ninth grade to help my daddy out—it’s been about nine months now. 

Yes, sir, nine months of this. And it’s not every single day, mind you. It comes and goes, on and off. Some weeks, it’s real quiet, and I think, well, maybe the storm has finally passed. I'll go down to the park and Hector just talks about his grandkids, and the porch is just an empty porch, and I can just rest my eyes in peace. But then, sure as the sun rises, it starts right back up again. So, to answer your question, no, it hasn't been my whole life, but it's been a good nine months, on and off, of carrying this around.
Do you ever feel like people are actively working together against you or trying to harm you in some way beyond just sending you warnings?

Well, now, let me just sit and ponder on that a second, doctor. Because, you know, a man has to be careful with his words when he's talking about other folks, especially in a small town like ours where everybody knows everybody else's business. You say the wrong thing to the wrong person, and before you know it, the whole congregation at First Baptist is praying for your soul on Sunday morning, and you didn't even do anything but sneeze too loud in the grocery store! 

But to answer what you're asking... no, I can't say I feel like anyone is out to get me or do me harm. I really don't. It's not like that at all. 

I mean, take Hector down at the park. Now, I told you he's slipping me those messages during the domino games, giving me the heads-up about things. But Hector? Hector wouldn't hurt a fly. I've known him for going on thirty years. I remember when his youngest daughter got married—oh, it must have been in the late nineties, maybe '98 or '99—and we all pitched in to help set up the folding chairs at the VFW hall because they couldn't afford a fancy country club wedding. He's a good man. He's just trying to warn me, that's all. He's trying to help me prepare for whatever it is that's coming. 

And the radio man, well, I don't even know his real name, but he doesn't sound angry or mean. He just sounds urgent, you know? Like a man trying to flag down a train before it hits a broken track. He's not trying to run me off the road or break into my house or anything like that. 

Nobody is sneaking around my yard at night or putting poison in my coffee. My wife makes the coffee every morning, anyway—she uses that store-brand stuff, says the name-brand is too bitter for her stomach these days, though I think it just tastes like hot brown water—and she certainly isn't trying to harm me. She just wants me to stop talking about the dominoes. 

So, no, doctor. It's just the warnings. Just folks trying to give an old man a heads-up. Nobody is plotting against me or trying to do me any kind of physical harm or ruin my life. I don't have enemies like that. I just have people trying to tell me things I need to know, even if I don't quite understand the whole picture yet.

Have you ever seen, heard, or felt things that others around you don't seem to notice, even when there was no actual person or event causing them, like hearing voices when no one is speaking or seeing things that aren't really there?

Well, now, doctor, I suppose that brings us right back around to Charlie, like I was mentioning just a little while ago. I know I touched on it, but since you're asking about hearing things when nobody is there... well, that's exactly what it is. 

You see, it usually happens in the afternoons. The mornings around our place are always a bit noisy, what with the wife clattering the breakfast dishes in the sink and having *The Price is Right* blaring on the television set because her hearing isn't quite what it used to be, bless her heart. But come two or three o'clock, she goes on back to the bedroom to lay down for a nap, and the house gets real quiet. Just... completely still, except for the ticking of the grandfather clock in the hallway that we got for our 40th anniversary. 

And some afternoons, when the house is quiet like that, I'll be sitting in my recliner, maybe looking at the newspaper or just resting my eyes, and plain as day, I hear my old friend call my name from out on the porch. Or sometimes he doesn't call my name, he just hums. He hums one of those old choir songs we used to sing at First Baptist—usually *In the Garden* or *How Great Thou Art*. 

And doctor, I tell you, it is so clear. It's not muffled like it's coming from a neighbor's open window, and it's not just a memory playing tricks in my head. It is clear like he is standing right there on the wooden boards of the porch, just waiting for me to come out with a couple glasses of sweet tea. I've gotten up and pushed open that screen door more times than I can count, fully expecting to see him sitting there in the green wicker chair. But... well, there's never anybody there. Just the empty porch and the dust floating around in the sunshine. But I hear him. I hear him just as clear as I'm hearing you right now, even when there's not a single soul around.
When you hear Charlie humming or calling your name, does it ever feel like the message has a hidden meaning, like it's trying to tell you something more than just a friendly greeting?

Well, now, Charlie’s humming... you know, that’s a thoughtful question, doctor. Let me just think on that a second. Charlie was always a straightforward fellow. When I hear him hum those old hymns, or call my name, it mostly just feels like... well, like he’s just keeping me company. Just letting me know he's around, sitting out there on the porch. 

But when you bring up hidden meanings and trying to tell me something more... see, that brings us right to the heart of the matter. That's exactly why I came to see you in the first place, doctor. Because it's not Charlie doing the warning, it's the others. Like I was mentioning earlier, I came because the men at the domino table—Hector and the boys—and sometimes that announcer on the radio, they are the ones giving those little messages meant just for me. 

I try to explain it to my wife, I really do. Just the other evening, we were having meatloaf—she makes it with those little crispy onions on top, which gives me terrible heartburn these days, but I eat it anyway because she works hard on it—and I caught one of those messages on the radio. I told her, I said, "Martha, did you catch that?" And she just waved her dish towel at me, like she was shooing away a horsefly. She always says it is just talk. Just regular old fellas shooting the breeze over dominoes or a man just reading the evening news. 

But I know better. Even when my wife says it is just talk, I know they are warning me to be careful. A man doesn't live to be eighty-four without learning how to read between the lines, you know? They slip these little warnings in, right under the surface of the regular conversation, and I know they're meant for me to be on my guard, even if Martha thinks I'm just a silly old man making a fuss over nothing at the dinner table.

Have you ever had times when you believed something was true that others around you didn't agree with, even when there was no evidence to support it, like believing you had special powers or that you were someone else entirely?

Well, now, special powers... that's a mighty big phrase, doctor. I wouldn't call it a superpower like you see in those comic books my grandson used to read—the ones with the fellows in the tight pants flying around. No, I wouldn't say I'm Superman or anything foolish like that. 

But... well, there are times, and it happens every so often, where I just get this feeling. This absolute certainty, deep down in my bones. It’s like a fire gets lit under me, and I just know—I get sure that I am the one who can bring the whole neighborhood together again. 

You see, our neighborhood isn't what it used to be. Back in the seventies, we used to have block parties every Fourth of July. The Johnsons would bring out their big charcoal grill, and my Martha would make her famous potato salad—the one with the little bit of mustard and paprika sprinkled on top. Everybody knew everybody. If a storm blew a branch onto your roof, three neighbors would be over with chainsaws before you even had time to put your boots on. But nowadays? Folks just pull their cars into their garages, hit the button to close the door, and you don't see them until the next morning. It's a crying shame, is what it is. 

But sometimes, I get this feeling that I have a special gift for fixing all that. I get to thinking that I have this... this knack for making people listen and follow my plans. I'll sit up half the night, drafting out these grand ideas. I'll draw up maps of the streets, figuring out where we can put up a big community tent, how we can organize a neighborhood watch that actually works, and how I'm going to be the one to stand up at the town hall meeting and get everybody fired up to be a real community again. 

I'll tell Martha about it, and I'll say, "Martha, I've got it all figured out. I know exactly how to make people see sense." And I feel so full of energy, like I could just march out the front door right then and there and start knocking on doors, and everybody would just fall in line because my ideas are so clear and perfect. But Martha, she just sighs and tells me to come to bed, says I'm getting myself worked up over nothing and that folks don't want to be bothered these days. She doesn't see it. She doesn't see that I have this... this calling, I suppose you could say, to be the one to lead everyone back together. It's just clear as a bell to me when it happens, even if nobody else quite understands the vision I have for us all.
Have you ever felt that you had a special mission, purpose, or role that no one else could fulfill, even when others didn't share your belief?

Well, now, doctor, that’s just exactly what I was getting at a second ago. A special mission... yes, sir, I suppose that’s a real good word for it. A mission. Like I was just saying, I get this... this absolute certainty that I am the only one who can bring this whole neighborhood together again. It’s not just a passing thought, you understand, it’s a real, deep-down purpose. 

I know I already chewed your ear off about the old block parties and Martha's potato salad, but you see, when this feeling hits me, it’s because I just know I have this special gift. It’s a gift for making people stop what they're doing, put down their yard tools or their groceries, and just listen to me. And not just listen, but actually follow my plans. 

I'll be sitting there at the kitchen table with my notebook—just a regular yellow legal pad I picked up from the pharmacy—and the plans just pour right out of me. It’s like I can see the whole street in my mind, every single house, from the Miller's place on the corner all the way down to the cul-de-sac where the pavement ends. And I think to myself, "If I just stand up on Mrs. Higgins' old oak tree stump in her front yard and lay it all out, they'll finally see." They'll see I have the vision. 

Nobody else is stepping up to do it, doctor. The young folks are too busy looking down at their telephones, and the older folks are too tired. But me? When that fire gets lit in me, I have the energy of a man half my age, and I have that gift to make them see how things ought to be. Martha says I'm just an old man dreaming and working myself into a lather over nothing, but a mission is a mission, whether your own wife believes in it or not. You understand what I mean? It’s a heavy thing, knowing you're the only one with the right plan to fix everything, and having the gift to make them follow it, even if folks like Martha don't quite see the picture yet.
Have you ever believed that you had a special connection to a higher power, or that you were chosen for a very important task that most people wouldn't understand?

Well, doctor, it seems like we keep circling the same wagon here, because like I’ve been trying to explain to you for the last few minutes, that’s exactly what’s happening with me. Chosen for an important task... yes, sir, that hits the nail right on the head. Now, I wouldn't go so far as to say I'm talking to burning bushes or anything like that—I'm a regular churchgoer, sure, but the Good Lord isn't sitting at the foot of my bed giving me orders. 

But I do get this feeling, like I keep saying. I just get so sure that I am the one—the only one—who can bring the whole neighborhood together again. And it really does feel like I've been chosen for it, because why else would I suddenly have this special gift for making people listen and follow my plans? I mean, think about it, doctor. I didn't even make it past the eighth grade. Back in those days, you had to go to work to help the family, so I was down at the lumber yard by the time I was fourteen, pulling my weight. I never went to college, never studied any of that politics or public speaking nonsense. 

So for an old man with my background to suddenly have all these brilliant ideas just pouring out... it has to be a special gift. I'll be sitting in my armchair, the one by the window where the draft comes in, and I can just picture it. I can picture myself standing up at the community center over on Elm Street—they painted it a terrible shade of yellow last spring, looks like a bruised banana if you ask me, but they do have a fine microphone setup—and I just know that if I start talking, folks will hang on my every word. They'll follow my plans to the letter. Most people wouldn't understand how a fellow like me could do it, and Martha certainly doesn't. She just tells me to drink my warm milk and rest my eyes. But you can't just rest your eyes when you know you've been chosen for something so important, when you have that gift to make folks listen. You just have to see it through.
Have you ever felt that your abilities or importance were much greater than they really were, like you had special powers, were destined for greatness, or had a special connection that others didn't?

Well, doctor, I... I feel like a broken record here, I really do. It's like we're just singing the same song but changing the verse, because, yes, sir, that's exactly what I've been trying to tell you this whole time. 

Destined for greatness, special powers, abilities being greater than they are... well, I don't know about "greater than they really are," because to me, it's as real as the chair I'm sitting in. But yes, it's just like I've been saying about the neighborhood. I get this... this overwhelming certainty, just out of the blue sometimes. I get sure that I am the one who can bring the whole neighborhood together again. 

And it's not just a passing fancy, it's like I have this special gift for making people listen and follow my plans. I mean, I told you about my background, pulling lumber since I was fourteen, never finishing school. So where would a man like me get the ability to just stand up and command a room? To draw up these grand plans on a yellow legal pad and know, deep in my heart, that folks will just fall in line? 

It's a gift, doctor. It's a special gift, and I know I have it, even if Martha thinks I'm just an old man talking out of turn. She doesn't see the importance of it. She doesn't see that when I get this feeling, I'm not just an eighty-four-year-old man with a bad knee—I'm the one who's going to fix things. I'm the one they're going to listen to. So, yes, I suppose you could say I feel my importance is pretty darn great when that fire gets lit under me. I just wish folks would listen instead of telling me to drink warm milk.
Have you ever believed that you were more important, powerful, or talented than others would say you are?

Doctor, I have to ask... is your hearing aid turned on? Or are you just testing my memory today? Because I swear on my mother's grave, we are beating a dead horse into the dirt right now. More talented? More important? Yes, sir, I've been telling you exactly that for the last twenty minutes! 

It's just like I've been saying. Folks look at me—folks like Martha, or the fellas down at the hardware store who just see an old man coming in to buy weatherstripping or a new box of nails—and they wouldn't say I'm anything special. They’d say I'm just an eighty-four-year-old retiree with a bad knee who ought to be sitting quiet in his armchair watching the television programs. 

But I know better. I get sure, right down to my marrow, that I am the one who can bring the whole neighborhood together again. They don't see the talent, but I know I have this special gift for making people listen and follow my plans. I mean, I sit there with my yellow pad, and the ideas are just so big, so important, they just flow right out of my pen. And if I were to just walk out there right now, down to where the Miller boy leaves his bicycle in the driveway every single afternoon—which is a terrible safety hazard, I might add, someone's going to trip and break a hip one of these days—and I just started speaking my mind, they would all see it too. 

They would see I'm not just some uneducated fellow who spent his life hauling lumber. They would see I have a real gift to make them follow my lead and fix this street up right. I don't know how many different ways I can explain the exact same thing to you, doc, but that's the long and short of it. I'm the one to do it, and I have the gift for it, no matter what anybody else might say.
Have you ever felt that your abilities or importance were much greater than others believed them to be?

Doc, are we... are we playing some sort of parlor game here? Because I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall. A very polite brick wall with a medical degree, sure, but a brick wall all the same! How many different ways can you ask a man the exact same question? 

Yes! Yes, I do! Like I have been telling you for the past half hour, others might look at me and just see a tired old man who didn't even finish middle school, a guy who spent his whole life breathing in sawdust down at the lumber yard. They believe my abilities amount to sitting in my armchair, staying out of the way, and maybe watering the geraniums if I'm feeling up to it. Martha certainly thinks that's the extent of my importance these days. 

But I know better. I get sure, I mean absolutely, one-hundred-percent sure, that I am the one who can bring the whole neighborhood together again.
